claims.text: Helm is a graduated Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF) project.
Helm charts are directories of templated YAML manifests, a `values.yaml` file of default inputs, and metadata.
The `helm` CLI renders chart templates using Go template syntax and either installs the resulting manifests into a cluster as a release or prints them to stdout.
Helm charts are distributed through Helm repositories and indexed publicly on Artifact Hub.
Helm is open source under the Apache License 2.0.
The Helm project does not ship a commercial tier.
Pulumi is open source under the Apache License 2.0.
Pulumi can manage any resource available in the Pulumi Registry, including AWS, Azure, Google Cloud, Kubernetes, Datadog, Cloudflare, GitHub, and Auth0; Helm manages Kubernetes resources only.
In Pulumi, resource ordering is derived from the dependency graph: each resource waits for its dependencies to become ready, and independent resources deploy in parallel.
Helm installs resources in a fixed order determined by Kubernetes kind, as defined in kind_sorter.go in the Helm source (pkg/release/v1/util/kind_sorter.go).
Helm chart authors cannot declare dependencies between resources or subcharts to control install order, except through hook weights.
Helm stores release metadata as Secrets (or ConfigMaps) inside the target Kubernetes cluster.
Pulumi state is managed by Pulumi Cloud by default; self-managed backends include Amazon S3, Azure Blob Storage, Google Cloud Storage, and local files.
Pulumi encrypts secrets in transit and at rest in the state file by default, with per-stack encryption keys and pluggable KMS providers (AWS KMS, Azure Key Vault, Google Cloud KMS, HashiCorp Vault).
Helm has no built-in secrets primitive; the community plugin `helm-secrets` exists for secrets handling.
A failed Pulumi update leaves the stack in a partially-updated state; `pulumi up` reconciles toward desired state and `pulumi refresh` detects drift.
`helm rollback` restores a release to a previous revision recorded in release history.
Pulumi's Automation API is a programmatic SDK in every supported language for embedding `up`, `preview`, and `destroy` in a host application.
The Helm SDK is available in Go only; other languages must shell out to the `helm` CLI.
Pulumi Packages let a component written in one language be consumed from any other language.
`pulumi import` and the `import` resource option both generate code in your language.
Helm has no direct equivalent of import, but existing in-cluster resources can be adopted into a release through resource ownership annotations.
Pulumi Policies is open source, with rules in Python, TypeScript, or Open Policy Agent Rego; Pulumi Cloud adds centralized policy management.
The Pulumi Enterprise edition adds Pulumi-maintained policy packs for CIS, PCI DSS, HITRUST, and NIST.
Helm has no native policy engine; policy is typically delegated to Kubernetes admission controllers such as Kyverno or OPA Gatekeeper.

The Helm docs state that "the Kubernetes objects from the charts and all its dependencies are aggregated into a single set; then sorted by type followed by name; and then created/updated in that order."

Helm's hardcoded kind order begins with PriorityClasses and Namespaces, then Secrets and ConfigMaps, then CustomResourceDefinitions and RBAC, then Services and workloads, with any kind not on the list (including custom resources) last.
Helm uninstall runs the same kind-sorted list in reverse.
Helm sends the sorted manifests to the API server in a single pass and does not wait for one resource to become ready before applying the next.
Helm chart dependencies are a packaging mechanism; a subchart's objects are merged into the parent chart's set and sorted by kind along with everything else.
Helm chart hooks ordered with `helm.sh/hook-weight` annotations are a workaround for ordering, and the hook resources are not managed by Helm as part of the release.
Native sequencing for resources and subcharts has been proposed in HIP-0025, which is still a draft.
In Pulumi, passing one resource's output into another, or setting the `dependsOn` resource option, creates an edge in the dependency graph.
The Pulumi Kubernetes provider waits for each resource to become ready before creating resources that depend on it, and deploys independent resources in parallel.
Pulumi deletes follow the dependency graph in reverse.
Pulumi's dependency-graph ordering with parallel deployment of independent resources makes updates faster than a strict serial sequence.

`helm.v4.Chart` in the Pulumi Kubernetes provider supports the `config.kubernetes.io/depends-on` annotation for ordering between objects inside the chart, and `dependsOn` on the chart for dependencies on resources outside it.
Pulumi programs written in general-purpose languages get typed inputs and outputs, loops, conditionals, classes, IDE features, and existing testing frameworks; Pulumi also supports YAML.

Pulumi manages non-Kubernetes resources and Kubernetes resources in one program through the Pulumi Registry, which covers AWS, Azure, Google Cloud, Kubernetes, and SaaS platforms like Datadog, Auth0, GitHub, and Cloudflare.
Helm records each install or upgrade as a numbered release revision.
Pulumi runs through the local CLI, programmatically through the Automation API, or remotely through Pulumi Deployments.
Helm favors fast revision-based rollback of a single release; Pulumi favors scriptable control over resources from many providers in one update.
Helm and Pulumi are commonly used in combination rather than as substitutes.
Two patterns cover most production deployments of Pulumi and Helm together.

A single Pulumi program can create the cluster (EKS, AKS, or GKE), configure networking and IAM, and install cert-manager, ingress-nginx, and external-dns through `helm.v4.Chart` or `helm.v3.Release`.
The Pulumi EKS guide walks through the pattern of creating a cluster and installing the operational stack end-to-end.
Pulumi resolves Helm chart values at deploy time and orders the chart install after the resources it depends on, so charts can consume infrastructure that did not exist when the program started.

Pulumi outputs (such as a database connection string from `aws.rds.Instance`, a KMS key ARN, a managed Redis endpoint, or a Cloudflare zone ID) can flow into a Helm chart's `values` input as typed Pulumi outputs.
The FAQ heading "What's the difference between `helm.Chart` and `helm.Release`?" exists on the page as an anchor target (#whats-the-difference-between-helmchart-and-helmrelease).
There are three common ways to adopt Pulumi alongside or in place of Helm, which can be combined.
Using Helm charts directly from a Pulumi program with `helm.v4.Chart` or `helm.v3.Release` is the most common Pulumi adoption pattern.
Rendering a chart with `helm template` and converting the YAML with `pulumi convert --from kubernetes` produces native Pulumi code.
`pulumi import` and the `import` resource option bring already-provisioned in-cluster resources under Pulumi management and generate the corresponding code.
The Pulumi Kubernetes provider exposes Helm charts as first-class resources through `helm.v4.Chart` and `helm.v3.Release`, and can pull charts from any Helm repository (public or private).

`helm.v4.Chart` renders chart templates locally and registers each Kubernetes object the chart produces as an individual Pulumi resource, so every child shows up in plan output, drift detection, and state.
`helm.v3.Release` uses the embedded Helm SDK and creates a real Helm release in the cluster, preserving chart hooks, post-rendering, and release history.

Helm merges the objects from a chart and all of its dependencies into a single set, sorts them by Kubernetes kind, and applies them in that order, so declaring a subchart as a dependency does not make it install first.
Pulumi creates and deletes resources in dependency order, with each resource ready before those that depend on it, rather than in a fixed order by kind.
